sections.h: A child asked for and given (1 Samuel 1–3)
sections.b: Samuel is born because Hannah asks God for a son and promises him back. His name is explained with the verb "ask" (1:20). Weaned, he is left at Shiloh to serve under Eli, wearing a linen ephod like a priest (2:18). While Eli's sons grow worse, Samuel grows "in the eyes of the LORD and of people too" (2:26). One night God calls him by name, and the boy's first message is the doom of Eli's house. By the end of chapter 3 all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knows him as a trustworthy prophet.

After the ark's disaster Samuel calls Israel to repent at Mizpah, prays and offers sacrifice while the LORD routs the Philistines (7:3–12). He judges Israel on a yearly circuit. When his own sons fail, the elders demand a king; Samuel takes it personally, but God tells him the people have rejected God, not Samuel (8:7). He warns them what a king will take, then anoints Saul in secret, presides over the lot at Mizpah and writes the rules of the kingdom (10:1, 10:17–25). Samuel holds several roles that later separate: prophet, priest-like sacrificer and judge.

common: Most readers see Samuel as a bridge figure, the last judge and the first of the prophets after Moses.
uncommon: Some critical scholars think Samuel's birth story was first told of Saul, since its naming pun fits Saul's name better.

claude.title: Two kinds of asking
claude.body: My own reading is that the verb "ask" ties Samuel's birth (1:20, 1:27) to the people's request for a king (8:10) and to Saul's name. Hannah asks and gives back; the people ask and want to keep. I suggest the book means the two askings as a contrast of faith and its opposite.

sections.b: Hannah is loved by her husband but childless and taunted every year by the other wife, Peninnah. At Shiloh she prays silently in her bitterness, and vows that a son will be given to the LORD for life. Eli thinks she is drunk. Her answer, "I have poured my soul out before the LORD" (1:15), is one of the Bible's great descriptions of prayer. When Samuel is born she keeps her vow, bringing him to Shiloh with a bull, flour and wine, and saying she has "handed him over" to the LORD (1:28).

Hannah's song celebrates a God who reverses fortunes: the strong fall and the weak are clothed in strength, the hungry are filled, the barren bears seven, the poor are seated with princes. It ends with a prayer for the LORD's king and his "anointed one," the first use of that title for a king in the Bible. Mary's song in Luke 1:46–55 is modeled on it. The Talmud learned rules of prayer from Hannah (Bavli Berakhot 31a–b).

common: Jewish tradition treats Hannah as the model of heartfelt prayer, and her story is read on Rosh Hashanah.
uncommon: Many critical scholars think the song was a royal psalm later placed in Hannah's mouth.

sections.b: Eli is priest at Shiloh and judges Israel forty years (4:18). He misreads Hannah's prayer, then blesses her; he raises Samuel and teaches him how to answer God's call (3:9). But he does not stop his sons Hophni and Phinehas, who steal from the sacrifices and despise the LORD's offering. A man of God tells him his family will lose the priesthood (2:27–36), and Samuel's first prophecy repeats it (3:11–14). Eli accepts the word: "He is the LORD" (3:18). Hearing that the ark is taken, the old, blind, heavy man falls backward and dies.

The oracle of 2:27–36 is fulfilled in stages: Hophni and Phinehas die on one day (4:11), Saul has the priests of Nob, Eli's descendants, killed (22:18–19), and Solomon removes Abiathar, the last survivor, from the priesthood in favor of Zadok (1 Kings 2:27, 35). Many readers identify the "faithful priest" of 2:35 with Zadok; some with Samuel; Christian readers with Christ.

common: Most readers see Eli as a sincere but weak father whose failure to restrain his sons cost his family the priesthood.
uncommon: The Talmud softens the charges against Eli's sons, saying they only delayed the women's offerings (Bavli Shabbat 55b).

sections.b: Saul, son of Kish, a wealthy Benjaminite, is tall and impressive. Sent to find lost donkeys, he meets Samuel, who has been told by God to anoint him ruler (9:16). The signs Samuel gives come true, the Spirit sweeps down on Saul, and he prophesies. Chosen by lot at Mizpah, he is found hiding among the baggage, then acclaimed king (10:17–24). When Nahash besieges Jabesh-gilead, the Spirit stirs Saul to muster Israel and win; he spares those who had despised him, and the kingdom is renewed at Gilgal (11:1–15).

These chapters show Saul at his best: modest (9:21), obedient to Samuel's directions, moved by the Spirit, merciful in victory (11:13). Readers differ on how much of his later failure is already hinted at: his hiding (10:22), his silence about the kingdom (10:16), the command to wait at Gilgal (10:8), and his choice for his looks (9:2; compare 16:7).

common: Most readers see chapters 9–11 as Saul's high point, before his failures in chapters 13–15.
uncommon: Some scholars read the book's whole portrait of Saul as shaped by David's court to justify David's takeover.

claude.title: Jabesh frames the reign
claude.body: I suggest the narrator frames Saul's reign with Jabesh-gilead: his first act as king rescues it (11:1–11), and its men rescue his body at the end (31:11–13).

sections.h: The ark taken and returned (1 Samuel 4–7)
sections.b: Israel brings the ark from Shiloh to the battle at Ebenezer, sure it will save them, but they are defeated and the ark is captured (4:1–11). In Philistine hands it topples the image of Dagon and brings plague on Ashdod, Gath and Ekron (5:1–12). The Philistines send it home on a cart pulled by two nursing cows, with a guilt offering of gold (6:1–12). At Beth-shemesh men die for looking into it, and it rests at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years (6:19–7:2). Many scholars think these chapters were once a separate "ark narrative." Leonhard Rost marked it as 4:1b–7:1 continued in 2 Samuel 6; Patrick Miller and J. J. M. Roberts argued it began with Eli's sons in chapter 2 and ended at 7:1.

common: Most readers take the lesson of chapter 4 to be that the ark could not be used to force God's help.
uncommon: Some scholars think the ark narrative was written to explain the fall of Shiloh to readers during the exile.

sections.h: Shiloh in the days of Eli (1 Samuel 1–4)
sections.b: Shiloh is Israel's central sanctuary at the start of 1 Samuel. Elkanah's family comes every year for a sacrifice and feast. The sanctuary is called "the LORD's temple" with a doorpost and doors (1:9; 3:15), and the ark stands there. Eli's sons serve as priests and abuse the worshipers. After the ark is lost in battle, Shiloh disappears from the story; later texts say God abandoned it (Psalm 78:60; Jeremiah 7:12–14). Excavations at Khirbet Seilun found a destruction layer in the eleventh century BC, which many connect with this time.

common: Most archaeologists date a destruction of Shiloh to around 1050 BC, matching the time of Eli.
uncommon: Some scholars think the shrine at Shiloh outlived the battle of Aphek and was destroyed later.

sections.h: The request for a king (1 Samuel 8)
sections.b: When Samuel's sons fail, Israel's elders ask for a king "like all the nations" (8:5). God tells Samuel they have rejected God himself as king (8:7), yet tells him to give them one. Samuel describes what the king will do: draft their sons, take their daughters, seize fields, tax a tenth of their crops and flocks, and make them slaves (8:11–17). Isaac Mendelsohn showed that this matches the practice of Canaanite kings known from Ugarit.

Saul is made king in three stages: anointed in secret by Samuel as "ruler" (nagid, 10:1), chosen publicly by lot at Mizpah (10:17–24), and confirmed at Gilgal after rescuing Jabesh (11:14–15). Samuel writes "the rules of the kingdom" in a scroll (10:25). Many critics see separate sources for and against kingship; others, such as Baruch Halpern, see a known pattern of designation, testing and confirmation.

common: Most readers agree that 1 Samuel holds both a positive and a critical view of kingship side by side.
uncommon: Some scholars argue that the anti-kingship passages were written after the fall of the monarchy.

sections.h: Philistine power in Samuel's day (1 Samuel 4–7; 9–10)
sections.b: The Philistines defeat Israel at Aphek and Ebenezer and capture the ark (4:1–11). Their five cities, Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron, each with a ruler (seren), act together (5:8; 6:4, 6:16–17). Their priests and diviners know the story of the exodus (4:8; 6:6). Samuel's victory at Mizpah holds them back (7:13), yet by Saul's time they have a post at Gibeah of God (10:5), and the rescue from them is the task God gives Saul (9:16).

common: Most historians link the Philistines to the Sea Peoples who settled the coast around 1175 BC.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Philistine league of five cities in 1 Samuel reflects a later period.

sections.b: The captured ark is placed beside Dagon in his temple at Ashdod. Twice Dagon falls face down before it; the second time his head and hands are broken off on the threshold (5:3–4). The narrator explains why Dagon's priests avoid stepping on the threshold "to this day" (5:5). The scene shows the LORD defeating a god on his own ground without any human help.

common: Most scholars now take Dagon as a grain or storm god of Syria, not a fish god.
uncommon: Some medieval and early modern readers took Dagon as half fish, from the Hebrew dag, "fish."

sections.b: Nahash king of Ammon besieges Jabesh-gilead and will make peace only if every man's right eye is put out (11:1–2). The paragraph preserved in the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a and known to Josephus, placed at 10:27 in the Plain, says he had already done this to the Gadites and Reubenites, and that seven thousand had fled to Jabesh. Saul's rescue of Jabesh is his first victory as king. Nahash later appears as a friend of David (2 Samuel 10:2).

common: Many text critics, following Cross, accept the Nahash paragraph of 4QSam-a as part of the earliest text.
uncommon: Some scholars, such as Alexander Rofé, regard it as an early expansion written to explain chapter 11.

sections.h: The word of the LORD returns (1 Samuel 3)
sections.b: "The LORD's word was rare in those days" (3:1). God calls Samuel by night, and from then on God's word is known through him: none of his words "drop to the ground" (3:19), and all Israel knows him as a prophet (3:20).

sections.h: Seers and bands of prophets (1 Samuel 9–10)
sections.b: In Saul's day a prophet is called a "seer" (9:9), someone consulted about lost property, with a small gift as a courtesy (9:6–8). Groups of prophets come down from a high place with music, in an ecstatic state (10:5, 10:10), and the Spirit makes Saul prophesy among them, giving rise to the proverb "Is Saul among the prophets too?" Similar ecstatic prophets are known from the letters of Mari.

common: Most scholars see two kinds of prophecy in these chapters: the single seer and the ecstatic group.
uncommon: Some think Samuel led the prophet bands as their "father" (10:12; 19:20).

sections.b: Hannah joins Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Samson's mother as a childless woman whose son becomes a turning point for Israel. The text twice says "the LORD had shut her womb" (1:5–6), and after her prayer "the LORD remembered her" (1:19). Her song turns her story into a rule of God's ways: "The childless woman bears seven" (2:5). She later has five more children (2:21).

Hannah vows that if God gives her a son, she will give him to the LORD for life, with no razor on his head (1:11), the mark of a Nazirite (Numbers 6:5; Judges 13:5). Elkanah confirms the vow (1:23), as a husband could under Numbers 30:10–15. Hannah keeps it at great cost, bringing the weaned child to Shiloh. The Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a makes the Nazirite vow explicit at 1:22.

common: Most readers see Samuel as a lifelong Nazirite, like Samson.
uncommon: The Mishnah records a rabbi who denied that Samuel was a Nazirite (Mishnah Nazir 9:5).

sections.b: The word mashiach, "anointed one," is first used of a king in Hannah's song: God will raise the horn of "his anointed one" (2:10). Samuel then pours oil on Saul's head (10:1), the first anointing of an Israelite king. From this rite comes the title "the LORD's anointed," used of Saul and David, and later the hope for a coming Messiah, the Christ.

common: Jewish and Christian readers both see 2:10 as an early root of messianic hope.

sections.h: Corrupt priests and a faithful priest (1 Samuel 2–3)
sections.b: Eli's sons take meat from sacrifices before the fat is burned and by force (2:12–17). The man of God's oracle announces that Eli's family, chosen in Egypt, will be cut off, and that God will raise "a faithful priest" (2:35). The oracle is read as fulfilled when Solomon replaces Abiathar with Zadok (1 Kings 2:27, 35). Samuel himself, though not of Aaron's line, wears an ephod and offers sacrifices.

sections.h: Ichabod: where is the glory? (1 Samuel 4)
sections.b: When the ark is captured and her husband and father-in-law are dead, Phinehas's wife names her newborn Ichabod, "no glory," saying "Glory has gone into exile from Israel" (4:21–22). The Hebrew word for glory (kavod) means weight, and the chapter plays on it: Eli is "heavy" (4:18), and the LORD's hand is "heavy" on the Philistines (5:6).

The Spirit of the LORD "sweeps down" on Saul, as on Samson, and he prophesies with the prophets (10:6, 10:10). The Spirit comes on him again to rouse him to rescue Jabesh (11:6). In these chapters the Spirit is a power for a task. Later the Spirit leaves Saul and comes on David (16:13–14).

At Mizpah Samuel brings the tribes forward and the lot falls on Benjamin, then the family of the Matrites, then Saul (10:20–21). The procedure is the one used to find Achan (Joshua 7:14–18), and later to expose Jonathan (14:41–42). When Saul cannot be found, the people ask the LORD again, and he tells them where Saul is hiding (10:22).

After the victory at Mizpah Samuel sets up a stone and names it Ebenezer, "stone of help," saying "Up to this point the LORD has helped us" (7:12). The name answers the defeat at another Ebenezer (4:1). The "big stone" at Beth-shemesh where the ark was set (6:14–18) was still pointed out in the writer's day; some scholars read 6:18 as calling it a "witness" ('ed for 'ad, "as far as").

sections.h: Samuel and the Dead Sea Scrolls
sections.b: The book of Samuel has more differences between its Hebrew text and its Greek translation than almost any other. Three scrolls from Qumran Cave 4, especially 4QSam-a, often agree with the Greek against the Masoretic Text. In 1 Samuel 1–11 the scroll supports a single three-year-old bull (1:24), Hannah's own spoken vow in place of the LORD's word (1:23), Eli's wish that God "repay" (2:20) and death by the sword for Eli's family (2:33), and preserves a paragraph about Nahash missing from all other texts (10:27). The Hebrew of Samuel seems to have been copied from a damaged or careless manuscript.

common: Most scholars agree that the Masoretic Text of Samuel has more scribal errors than most biblical books.
uncommon: A few scholars think 4QSam-a represents a separate edition of Samuel rather than a better copy.

sections.b: The title "the LORD of Armies" (YHWH tseva'ot, traditionally "LORD of hosts") first appears in the Bible at 1:3, linked with Shiloh and the ark (4:4). Hannah is the first person in the Bible to address God by it in prayer (1:11). The "armies" may be Israel's, the stars, or the angels; the title presents God as king enthroned on the cherubim.

Samuel tells Israel to return to the LORD with all their heart and put away the Baals and Ashtoreths (7:3). At Mizpah they draw water and pour it out, fast and confess, "We have sinned against the LORD" (7:6). God answers with thunder and victory, the pattern of Judges at its best.

Saul's home is Gibeah of Benjamin, the town of the outrage in Judges 19. After his choosing he goes home to Gibeah with men God had touched in their hearts (10:26), and there he hears of Jabesh (11:4). Gibeah is often identified with Tell el-Ful, north of Jerusalem, where a small fortress has been dug.

Eli is said to have judged Israel forty years (4:18), and Samuel judges Israel all his life on a circuit of Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah (7:15–17). The pattern of Judges continues: Israel serves Baals, the Philistines oppress, the people repent, and God rescues. Saul's rescue of Jabesh is told like a judge's victory (11:6–11).

sections.h: Sacrifice at Shiloh and the high places (1 Samuel 1–2; 9)
sections.b: Elkanah's family offers a yearly sacrifice and shares the meat (1:3–5). Eli's sons break the rules for the priests' share and the fat (2:13–17). Samuel offers a nursing lamb at Mizpah (7:9) and blesses a sacrifice at a high place before the meal (9:13), where Saul is given the thigh, a priestly portion (9:24).

sections.h: A day of fasting at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:6)
sections.b: At Mizpah the people pour out water before the LORD, go without food for the day, and confess, "We have sinned against the LORD," while Samuel prays for them (1 Samuel 7:5–6). The fast is part of a national day of repentance, and the Philistine attack that follows is turned back (7:7–11).
